title: First contact: read your dispatch
concept: This is a terminal: you type a command, press Enter, and Linux prints the result. Your first command is cat, which prints the contents of a text file to the screen. Reading a file with cat never changes it.
brief: Your home directory holds a file called dispatch.txt. Read it to find your first flag.

files.text: Welcome, operator. Your first dispatch contains {{FLAG}}
Hello! Your mission file is dispatch.txt. Use cat to read it.

hints: The command is cat, a space, then the filename.
Run cat dispatch.txt, then highlight the CYBER{...} text in the output.
example: cat notes.txt      # prints everything inside notes.txt
explanation: Every command starts with its name, followed by any arguments, separated by spaces. Here, cat is the command and the filename is its argument. The text before the $ (user@cybercodex:~) is the prompt. It shows who you are and where you are, and you don't type it. The ~ means your home directory, which is where every mission starts unless it says otherwise.
pitfall: Don't type the $ or anything before it. That's the prompt, not part of the command. And don't run the flag as a command: paste it into the flag box.
transfer: What would happen if you ran cat dispatch.txt twice? Would the file change?
steps: Type cat dispatch.txt and press Enter.
Find the flag in the output. It looks like CYBER{...}.
Highlight the whole flag with your mouse (it copies automatically) and paste it into the flag box.
why: Security work starts with reading: config files, logs, notes left on a system. cat is the quickest way to look inside a file.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.
Filenames include their extension. Run ls to see the exact name (dispatch.txt).
Commands are case sensitive. Use lowercase: cat

title: Know your operator
concept: Linux always knows which user is running each command. whoami prints your username, and id adds your numeric user ID (UID) and your groups.
brief: Dispatches are sorted by username. Find out who you are, then read the dispatch addressed to you.

files.text:
ACCESS DENIED: this dispatch is addressed to admin, not you.
Run whoami to check which user you are.

This guest account was retired last year. Nothing for you here.
Run whoami to check which user you are.

hints: whoami prints user.
Run cat dispatches/user.txt. The other files belong to other people.
example:
whoami      # prints your username
id          # prints your UID, GID and groups
explanation: Your username is the human-friendly name. The UID is the number Linux actually uses to decide what you may read or change. Groups give extra access to shared files. This lab has one practice user, user, so nothing you do here touches your real computer or anyone else's environment.
pitfall: The user shown in the lab isn't your CyberCodex account or email. It's the practice user inside your environment.
transfer: How is a username different from a UID, and why would Linux use the number?
steps: Run whoami to find your username.
Run ls dispatches to see who has mail.
Read the file named after your username: cat dispatches/<your username>.txt
why: On any system you break into or defend, the first question is "who am I running as?". Your user decides what you can access.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.
Dispatches now live in the dispatches folder. Try ls dispatches.

title: Your place in the tree
concept: pwd (print working directory) shows exactly where you are in the filesystem, as a full path that starts with /.
brief: You've been dropped into the field somewhere. Work out where you are, then read the coordinates file in that exact spot.

files.text:
Wrong sector. These are sector 2's coordinates.
The mission started you somewhere else; pwd tells you where you were.

These are headquarters' coordinates, not yours.
You were dropped in the field. Go back with cd - or cd ~/field/sector-4

hints: pwd shows /home/user/field/sector-4.
Just run cat coordinates.txt without moving. The copy in your home folder is for HQ.
example:
pwd         # prints something like /home/user
ls          # lists what's in that directory
explanation: The Linux filesystem is one big tree. The very top is the root, written as /. Whenever you type a filename without a leading /, Linux looks for it in the directory pwd shows. That's why the same command can read different files depending on where you're standing.
pitfall: A path tells you where something lives. coordinates.txt here and /coordinates.txt at the root would be two different files.
transfer: Why might cat notes.txt work in one directory but fail in another?
steps: Run pwd. This mission does NOT start in your home folder.
Run ls to see what's here.
Read coordinates.txt right where you are.
why: When a command says "No such file", checking pwd is the first thing to do. Most of the time you're simply in the wrong place.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.

title: The dispatch shelf
concept: ls lists the files in a directory. Files whose names start with a dot (like .config) are hidden from a normal listing. ls -a shows everything, and ls -l shows details like permissions and size.
brief: Something is hidden in your home directory. List everything, find the hidden dispatch and read it.

files.text: Not all files appear in a normal listing.
Nothing useful in here. Hidden files never show up in a plain ls.
Temporary session data. Not the dispatch.

hints: Try ls -a.
The hidden file is called .dispatch. Run cat .dispatch.
example:
ls          # normal listing
ls -a       # include hidden files (names starting with .)
ls -l       # long listing with permissions and sizes
explanation: Options such as -a and -l change how a command behaves. Hidden files are just a naming convention to reduce clutter, not a security feature: anyone who knows the name, and has permission, can read them. Remember that filenames are case sensitive, so Notes.txt and notes.txt are different files.
pitfall: The dot is part of the filename, so cat dispatch won't work. Listing a file also doesn't show its contents; you still need cat.
transfer: Does hiding a file with a dot stop another user from reading it?
steps: Run ls and notice that only readme.txt appears.
Run ls -a to reveal hidden files.
Read the hidden file with cat (keep the dot in its name).
why: Attackers and admins both stash things in dotfiles. Always use ls -a when you're exploring a system.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.
Hidden files keep their dot. The name is .dispatch

title: Walk to the relay
concept: cd (change directory) moves you to another directory. cd .. goes up one level, cd - jumps back to where you just were, and plain cd takes you home.
brief: Three stations, one message. Walk into the relay station, read its message, then head back home.

files.text:
Wrong station! This is the depot.
The relay is next door: cd ../relay

Wrong station! This is the tower.
The relay is next door: cd ../relay

hints: Run ls to see the stations directory.
From home, cd stations/relay takes you straight there.
example:
cd /tmp     # go to /tmp
pwd         # confirm where you are
cd -        # jump back to the previous directory
explanation: Your terminal remembers one current directory. After a cd, every filename you type is looked up from the new location. Directories inside directories are written with / between them, so stations/relay means "the relay folder inside stations". Use pwd or ls after moving if you want to check where you landed.
pitfall: cd doesn't print anything when it works. No output means success, so run pwd if you want to check.
transfer: What's the difference between cd .. and cd /?
steps: Run ls stations to see the three stations.
Move in with cd stations/relay (Tab completes the names).
Read message.txt, then run cd on its own to go home.
why: Moving around the filesystem quickly is the core skill for every later mission and every real system you'll work on.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.
message.txt isn't in this folder. Run pwd and ls. The messages live inside each station.
There's no relay folder here. It's inside stations: cd stations/relay

title: Read without moving
concept: An absolute path starts with / and points to the same place no matter where you are. You can read a file anywhere by giving cat its absolute path, without moving.
brief: A dispatch is waiting in /opt/academy. Read it without leaving your home directory.

files.text:
Out-of-date local copy!
The live dispatch is at the absolute path /opt/academy/dispatch.txt (note the leading slash).

hints: Start the path with /.
Run cat /opt/academy/dispatch.txt.
example: cat /etc/hostname      # read a file by its absolute path
explanation: So far you've used relative paths, which start from your current directory. Absolute paths start from the root /. They're handy in instructions and scripts because they always work, whatever directory the terminal happens to be in.
pitfall: The leading slash matters. opt/academy/dispatch.txt (no slash) would look inside your current directory instead.
transfer: How could you read a file in another directory without going into it?
steps: Stay in your home directory (no cd needed).
Run cat /opt/academy/dispatch.txt.
Optional: run pwd to confirm you never moved.
why: Logs and config files live in fixed places like /var/log and /etc. Reading them by absolute path is something you'll do constantly.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.
This mission is about reading without moving. Try cat with the full path from /.

title: Ask the manual
concept: You don't have to memorize every command. man COMMAND opens a command's manual, and help lists every command this lab supports.
brief: Use the manual for ls to learn how to show hidden files, then use that to find the hidden receipt in /opt/academy/helpdesk.

files.text: The receipt is hidden in this folder. man ls explains how to see hidden files.
Ticket closed: printer on fire. Not related to your receipt.

hints: man ls shows that -a includes hidden entries.
Run ls -a /opt/academy/helpdesk, then cat /opt/academy/helpdesk/.receipt.
example:
help        # list every supported command
man cat     # read the manual for cat
explanation: Real professionals look things up constantly. Read a manual's first line to see the basic syntax, then try one option at a time. This lab's manuals describe its supported subset; on a full Linux system, man pages are longer and cover more options.
pitfall: Not every command or option you see online exists here. If one isn't supported, the lab will tell you, so check man first.
transfer: How would you check whether an option is supported before using it?
steps: Run man ls and look for the option that shows hidden entries.
List /opt/academy/helpdesk with that option.
Read the hidden file by its full path.
why: Knowing how to find the answer is more valuable than memorizing it. Every tool you meet later will come with a manual.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.

title: One floor up
concept: A relative path can climb up with .. before going back down. ../store/receipt.txt means "go up one level, enter store, then find receipt.txt".
brief: You're standing in the work directory. The receipt is in the store directory next door. Read it without using an absolute path.

files.text: Supplies are in the store, which is next door to work (one level up, then into store).

Wrong store! This is the supply closet inside work.
The real store is next door: ../store/receipt.txt

hints: Read the note in work first.
.. climbs out of work, so cat ../store/receipt.txt reads the store next door.
example:
cat ../notes.txt          # a file one level above you
cat ./notes.txt           # a file right here (same as notes.txt)
explanation: This mission starts you inside /home/user/work. The . in a path means "here" and .. means "the parent directory", and they can appear anywhere in a path. If a path confuses you, resolve it one piece at a time: start at pwd, then apply each part in order.
pitfall: ../store is not /store. The first depends on where you are; the second always starts at the root.
transfer: Starting in /home/user/work, where does ../../ point to?
steps: Run pwd to confirm you're in /home/user/work.
Run ls .. to see the directories next to work.
Read the receipt with cat ../store/receipt.txt.
why: Relative paths keep commands short and portable. You'll see ../ in scripts, configs and exploits all the time.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.

title: Names with spaces
concept: The shell splits what you type into separate words at spaces. To use a filename that contains a space, wrap it in quotes so it stays one argument.
brief: Someone saved the shift notes with a space in the filename. Read shift notes.txt.

files.text:
This is the shift roster, not the notes. Did cat read two files?
Without quotes, cat shift notes.txt means two files: shift and notes.txt
These are someone else's notes. You want the single file called "shift notes.txt"

hints: Run cat shift notes.txt without quotes and read what it prints.
Wrap the whole name in quotes: cat "shift notes.txt"
example:
cat "my report.txt"      # one file whose name has a space
cat my report.txt        # two files: my and report.txt
explanation: Without quotes, cat shift notes.txt asks for two files: shift and notes.txt. Quotes keep the whole name together, and the shell removes them before cat sees the name. Double quotes and single quotes both work for this. Single quotes are completely literal, which matters once you meet variables.
pitfall: Tab completion can add a backslash before the space for you. That works too.
transfer: Why is cat "a b.txt" different from cat a b.txt?
steps: Run ls to see the filename.
Read it with cat "shift notes.txt" (including the quotes).
why: Real systems are full of awkward filenames, especially anything copied from Windows or macOS. Quoting correctly prevents some nasty mistakes.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.

title: Copy a field report
concept: cp copies a file and leaves the original where it is. mkdir creates a new directory. A copy needs its destination directory to exist first.
brief: Make a backup of the field report: create a backup directory and copy report.txt into it. Your flag appears in reward.txt once the backup is in place.
hints: Create the folder first with mkdir backup.
The backup must end up at /home/user/backup/report.txt.
example:
mkdir copies                      # create a folder
cp notes.txt copies/notes.txt     # copy a file into it
explanation: A copy is a completely separate file with the same contents, so changing one later won't affect the other. cp won't create missing directories for you, so make the folder first with mkdir. This mission checks your filesystem: once the backup exists with the right contents, a reward.txt file containing your flag appears in your home directory.
pitfall: Copying onto an existing file replaces its contents with no warning. Check the destination carefully.
transfer: When would you choose cp instead of mv?
steps: Run mkdir backup.
Run cp report.txt backup/report.txt.
Read the reward with cat reward.txt.
why: Backing up a file before you touch it is a habit that saves careers, especially when you're editing configs on a live system.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.
cp won't create folders for you. Make it first with mkdir backup.
mv moves the original away. The task wants a copy, so report.txt should stay put. Use cp.

title: Rename the incoming report
concept: mv moves or renames a file. Unlike cp, the old name disappears, because it's the same file under a new path.
brief: The incoming report has been approved. Rename incoming.txt to approved.txt, keeping its contents, and collect your reward.
hints: Both files are in your home directory.
Run mv incoming.txt approved.txt.
example:
mv draft.txt final.txt       # rename a file
mv final.txt reports/        # move it into a folder
explanation: Renaming and moving are the same operation in Linux: you're changing the path used to reach the file. mv old.txt new.txt renames it, and mv file.txt folder/ moves it into a folder. Afterwards, check that the old name is gone. Once the rename is correct, reward.txt appears with your flag.
pitfall: If incoming.txt still exists afterwards, you copied the file instead of moving it.
transfer: How could you prove you moved a file rather than copied it?
steps: Run mv incoming.txt approved.txt.
Run ls to check that incoming.txt is gone.
Read the reward with cat reward.txt.
why: Renaming files is everyday admin work, and knowing the difference between moving and copying avoids lost or duplicated data.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.
cp makes a copy, so incoming.txt still exists. This task needs a rename: use mv (you can rm the copy).

title: Beginner checkpoint: locate the parcel
concept: Checkpoint time: no new commands, just everything from chapters 1 to 3 combined. Work methodically: get to the right place, look at everything there (including hidden files), then read what you find.
brief: Checkpoint. A parcel is hidden in /opt/academy/relay/archive. Watch out: it isn't the only parcel on the relay.

files.text: Parcel #4471, delivered to the relay archive: {{FLAG}}
The parcel is hidden, not missing.

hints: Hidden files need ls -a.
The parcel is called .parcel.
example:
cd /some/place     # go there
ls -a              # look at everything, hidden files included
explanation: Investigations go faster when you split them into steps. First, where am I and where do I need to be? Second, what's here, including hidden entries? Third, which file is the one I want? Read the output carefully and separate the flag from the prompt and the other text.
pitfall: Copy only the CYBER{...} flag, not the text around it. Flags from a reset environment no longer count.
transfer: Could you reach the same parcel with both a relative path and an absolute path?
steps: Go to /opt/academy/relay/archive.
List everything there, including hidden files.
Read the hidden parcel in that folder, not anywhere else.
why: This is how real exploration works: navigate, enumerate, read. You'll repeat this loop on every machine you investigate.

decoys.hint: That's the staging parcel from /opt/academy/relay. The task asked for the one inside the archive folder.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.

title: Search the relay log
concept: grep prints only the lines that contain your search text. It's the fastest way to find one line in a huge log. Matching is case sensitive unless you add -i, and you can search for a phrase by putting it in quotes.
brief: Somewhere in /var/log/relay.log is the receipt that was ACCEPTED. Other receipts were voided. The log was rotated, so relay.log.1 holds last week's entries.

files.text:
boot ready
status ok
RECEIPT VOID {{DECOY:0}}
status waiting
receipt pending (lowercase entries are previews)
RECEIPT ACCEPTED {{FLAG}}
status ok

hints: grep RECEIPT /var/log/relay.log shows more than one receipt.
Search for the phrase: grep "RECEIPT ACCEPTED" /var/log/relay.log
example:
grep ERROR app.log              # lines containing ERROR
grep "disk full" app.log        # search for a phrase
explanation: Logs are written one event per line, so grep turns thousands of lines into the few you care about. Search for the most specific text you know. If you get several matches, read them and refine the search, for example by searching for a longer phrase.
pitfall: Case matters unless you select -i. The search pattern and filename are separate arguments.
transfer: How would you display every line except those containing DEBUG?
steps: Search the current log for RECEIPT and read every match.
Narrow the search to the accepted receipt only.

decoys.hint: That receipt was VOID. Read the whole line: you need the ACCEPTED one.
That's from relay.log.1, last week's rotated log. The task is about the current /var/log/relay.log.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.
grep is case sensitive. The log writes RECEIPT in capitals (or use grep -i).

title: Locate a filename
concept: find searches a whole directory tree for files by name, however deep they're buried. find /some/path -name parcel.txt prints every match.
brief: A parcel addressed to you is somewhere in the depot under /opt/academy. More than one parcel.txt is in there.

files.text: Shipment received. Parcels are stored by aisle and bin.

hints: find /opt/academy -name parcel.txt
Check who each parcel is for. Yours says 'for: user'.
example:
find /home -name "*.txt"        # every .txt file below /home
find /etc -name hosts           # files named exactly hosts
explanation: Clicking through folders one at a time doesn't scale. find walks every folder below the path you give it. When find returns several matches, check each one, because files with the same name can mean very different things.
pitfall: A filename match does not mean the file contains the desired record. Inspect it after discovery.
transfer: When would you use find first and grep second?
steps: Use find to list every parcel.txt below /opt/academy.
Read them and keep the one addressed to user.

decoys.hint: That parcel is addressed to admin. Read the 'Parcel for:' line and find the one for user.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.

title: Inspect a batch with globbing
concept: A glob is a wildcard pattern the shell expands into matching filenames. *.txt means every name ending in .txt, so cat batches/*.txt reads them all in one go.
brief: The batches folder mixes .txt batches with log files and an archive. The receipt is in one of the .txt batches directly inside batches.
hints: cat batches/*.txt
Only top-level .txt files count; the archive folder and .log files are distractions.
example:
ls *.log           # every .log file here
cat report-?.txt   # report-1.txt, report-2.txt, ...
explanation: The shell expands the pattern before the command runs, so cat simply receives a list of files. * matches any characters except /, which means it never reaches into subfolders. ? matches exactly one character.
pitfall: Quoting the wildcard prevents shell expansion. Dotfiles require an explicit dot in the pattern.
transfer: What different sets of names do *.txt and ?.txt select?
steps: Read every .txt file directly inside batches with one glob.
Ignore logs and anything in subfolders.

decoys.hint: That came from c.log, a log file. The task asked for the .txt batches.
That's from the archive subfolder. The task wants the batches directly inside batches (*.txt doesn't go into subfolders).

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.

title: Select the last dispatch
concept: head shows the first lines of a file and tail shows the last lines. Add -n NUMBER to choose how many.
brief: dispatches.txt is a running log. The newest dispatch is always added at the bottom. Don't trust the header.
hints: The header line contains a sample flag. It is not the newest dispatch.
tail -n 1 dispatches.txt
example:
head -n 3 app.log     # first three lines
tail -n 1 app.log     # the very last line
explanation: Logs grow at the bottom, so the newest entry is always the last line. tail -n 1 gives you just that. head is handy for a quick peek at a file's format without printing all of it.
pitfall: tail -n 1 selects one line, not one character.
transfer: Which command would you use to inspect a file header?
steps: Peek at the top with head to see what kind of file it is.
Print only the newest (last) line.

decoys.hint: That's the sample entry from the header at the top. The newest dispatch is the last line (tail).

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.

title: Filter the signal
concept: A pipe | sends one command's output into the next command. You can chain filters: grep DELIVER keeps matching lines, and grep -v TEST throws away lines containing TEST.
brief: stream.log contains several DELIVER lines, but only one is a live delivery. The others are TEST deliveries. Use a pipeline to isolate the live one.
solution: cat stream.log | grep DELIVER | grep -v TEST
hints: cat stream.log | grep DELIVER shows the test lines too.
cat stream.log | grep DELIVER | grep -v TEST
example:
cat app.log | grep ERROR             # keep errors
cat app.log | grep ERROR | grep -v debug   # ...but drop debug lines
explanation: Each command in a pipeline does one small job. Chaining them lets you narrow output step by step without creating temporary files. Read your output after each step and add a filter only when you need one.
pitfall: Do not add a filename to the receiving command unless you intend it to read that file instead of the pipe.
transfer: Why is a pipe different from running two commands separated by a semicolon?
steps: Pipe stream.log into grep to keep DELIVER lines.
Add a second filter that removes TEST lines.

decoys.hint: That was a TEST delivery. Filter those out with grep -v TEST.
That was a TEST delivery. Filter those out with grep -v TEST.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.

title: Write a report
concept: > sends a command's output into a file instead of the screen. It creates the file, or completely replaces whatever was in it.
brief: status.txt still says the relay is offline. Replace its contents with exactly: relay ready
hints: echo "relay ready" > status.txt
Use >, not >>. >> would keep the old line.
example: echo "all good" > status.txt     # status.txt now contains: all good
explanation: echo prints text, and echo "text" > file.txt writes that text into file.txt. The file must end up containing exactly the right text, so watch spelling and capitals. Once it matches, reward.txt appears.
pitfall: Avoid cat sample.txt > sample.txt. Use a separate temporary destination.
transfer: Why can > destroy data even when the command itself is only reading?
steps: Check the current contents with cat status.txt.
Overwrite it with the new status using echo and >.
Read reward.txt.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.
>> adds to the end of the file. To replace the contents, use a single >.

title: Append without erasing
concept: >> adds output to the end of a file and keeps everything already there. A single > would wipe the file first.
brief: status.log says offline. Add a second line, restored, without losing the first.
hints: echo restored >> status.log
If you used a single >, the first line is gone. Put it back with echo offline > status.log, then append.
example: echo "next entry" >> journal.log    # adds a line at the bottom
explanation: Logs and notes grow over time, so you almost always want >> when adding to them. Mixing up > and >> is one of the most common ways people lose data on Linux.
pitfall: Using > instead of >> replaces the entire previous log.
transfer: How would the output differ if you appended the same record twice?
steps: Read status.log.
Append the word restored as a new line.
Check the file has both lines, then read reward.txt.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.
Careful: a single > replaces the whole file. Check status.log. If 'offline' is gone, restore it first.

title: Separate repeated messages
concept: uniq removes repeated lines, but only when the repeats sit next to each other. sort first to bring duplicates together, then uniq -u keeps only the lines that appear exactly once.
brief: messages.txt is full of repeated messages. Exactly one line appears only once, and that's your flag. Some repeats are far apart.
hints: uniq only compares neighbouring lines.
sort messages.txt | uniq -u
example:
sort names.txt | uniq -c     # count each name
sort names.txt | uniq -u     # names that appear only once
explanation: This is a classic trap: uniq on an unsorted file misses duplicates that are far apart. sort | uniq is the standard pairing. -u shows lines that appear once, and -c counts how many times each appears.
pitfall: sort changes order. Do not use it when the original sequence carries meaning you must preserve.
transfer: Why does uniq without sort sometimes leave repeated values?
steps: Try uniq -u on the file directly and notice something's off.
Sort first, then keep only the unique lines.

decoys.hint: That line actually appears twice; the copies just aren't next to each other. Sort first: sort messages.txt | uniq -u

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.

title: Extract a manifest field
concept: cut pulls one column out of each line. -d sets the separator and -f picks the field number, so cut -d : -f 3 gives the third colon-separated field.
brief: manifest.txt lists shipments as id:status:payload. Extract the payload (field 3) of the shipment whose status is ready.
hints: The first line is a header, and one shipment is on hold.
grep :ready: manifest.txt | cut -d : -f 3
example:
cut -d : -f 1 /etc/passwd           # every username
grep root /etc/passwd | cut -d : -f 7  # root's shell
explanation: Lots of system files are colon-separated (like /etc/passwd). Combine cut with grep to pick a row first and then the column you need. Fields are counted from 1.
pitfall: If a delimiter appears inside a quoted value, this simple cut command still treats it as a delimiter.
transfer: What does field 1 mean when there is no delimiter on the line?
steps: Look at the file to see its columns.
Select the ready row, then cut out field 3.

decoys.hint: That payload belongs to shipment 1001, which is on hold. You need the ready one.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.

title: Decode the shipment label
concept: Base64 turns any data into plain letters and numbers so it can travel safely through text systems. It's an encoding, not encryption: base64 -d turns it straight back.
brief: The shipment label in label.b64 is base64-encoded. Decode it. (Ignore old-label.b64: that shipment has been delivered.)
hints: Submitting the encoded text won't work. Decode it first.
base64 -d label.b64
example:
echo aGVsbG8= | base64 -d     # prints: hello
base64 -d file.b64            # decode a whole file
explanation: Base64 text looks scrambled, often ends in = signs, and shows up constantly in security work (tokens, email attachments, malware). Recognising it and decoding it is a core skill.
pitfall: Copying only part of an encoded line can cause an invalid-input error.
transfer: Why should a password not be protected with base64 alone?
steps: Look at label.b64. Notice it's encoded.
Decode it with base64 -d.

decoys.hint: That's from old-label.b64, a delivered shipment. Decode label.b64 instead.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.

title: Recover read permission
concept: Every file has permissions: read (r), write (w) and execute (x). If you can't read a file, chmod u+r gives you (the owner) read permission back.
brief: sealed.txt holds your flag, but nobody can read it. Diagnose the permissions, fix them and read the file. The copy is not what it seems.

files.text: Nice try! This copy was made before the flag was added. Fix sealed.txt's permissions instead.

hints: ls -l sealed.txt shows the owner can write but not read.
chmod u+r sealed.txt, then cat sealed.txt
example:
ls -l secret.txt         # --w------- means no read permission
chmod u+r secret.txt     # give the owner read access
explanation: ls -l shows permissions as a string like -rw-r--r--. The first three letters after the dash are the owner's. A dash means that permission is missing. Permission errors are among the most common problems on real systems, and fixing them is a basic admin skill.
pitfall: File readability and parent-directory traversal are separate requirements.
transfer: What is preserved when you add u+r rather than replace the mode with an octal value?
steps: Try to read sealed.txt and note the error.
Inspect its permissions, then give yourself read access.
Read it.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.
Permission denied means you lack read access. Check with ls -l sealed.txt and fix it with chmod u+r.

title: Intermediate checkpoint: process a manifest
concept: A pipeline can combine selection, field extraction, and decoding. Inspect each stage separately if you are unsure what data it produces.
brief: Checkpoint. /var/log/manifest holds encoded records as NAME:payload. Decode the payload of the record named exactly READY. Similar records and an old manifest are there to trip you up.
hints: grep READY matches READY_TEST too. Include the colon: grep READY: /var/log/manifest
grep READY: /var/log/manifest | cut -d : -f 2 | base64 -d
example: grep READY example.txt | cut -d : -f 2
explanation: Complex pipelines are easier to debug incrementally. Run the first stage and inspect its output. Add a second stage and check the shape again. Decode only the payload, not the record label. If a stage outputs nothing, inspect that stage before adding more commands.
pitfall: Including the READY: prefix in the base64 decoder input will not produce the intended message.
transfer: Which intermediate output would you inspect first if decoding failed?
steps: Find the record named exactly READY (look at what else starts with READY).
Cut out its payload and decode it, ideally in one pipeline.

decoys.hint: That came from the READY_TEST record. You need the record named exactly READY.
That's from manifest.old. Use the current /var/log/manifest.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.

title: Read through standard input
concept: < feeds a file into a command's standard input, as if you'd typed its contents. base64 -d < file.b64 decodes without passing the filename as an argument.
brief: Decode the current receipt by feeding receipt.b64 into base64 with input redirection. An older receipt is lying around too.
hints: base64 -d < receipt.b64
receipt-2023.b64 is expired.
example:
wc -l < access.log        # count lines read from stdin
base64 -d < data.b64      # decode from stdin
explanation: Many tools read from standard input when no file is given. < lets you plug any file into them, and it's the mirror image of >. You'll use it with tools that only read stdin, and in scripts.
pitfall: The arrow points from the file into the command. > points output toward a destination file.
transfer: Can you explain the data flow of wc -l < sample.log > count.txt?
steps: Decode receipt.b64 using < rather than a filename argument.

decoys.hint: That's the expired 2023 receipt. Decode receipt.b64.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.

title: Keep a copy of the evidence
concept: tee writes its input to a file and also passes it on to the screen, so you can save evidence while still seeing it. ^ in a grep pattern means the line must start with that text.
brief: Save exactly the line from source.log that starts with OK into evidence.txt, and watch it print as you do. Lines that merely contain OK don't count.

files.text:
NO pending
NOT OK checksum failed
OK relay restored
NO retry

hints: grep OK source.log also matches NOT OK.
grep ^OK source.log | tee evidence.txt
example: grep ^ERROR app.log | tee errors.txt
explanation: When you investigate, keep exact copies of what you found. tee lets you save a pipeline's output without breaking the pipeline. Anchors like ^OK prevent accidental matches such as NOT OK.
pitfall: tee does not filter the input. Perform selection before tee if you only want selected records saved.
transfer: Where would you place tee to inspect the output of a middle pipeline stage?
steps: Find the line that starts with OK (not lines like NOT OK).
Save exactly that one line to evidence.txt with tee.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.

title: Spot a changed line
concept: diff compares two files line by line. Lines starting with < come from the first file and lines starting with > from the second.
brief: Compare before.txt and after.txt. One line was edited and one line was added at the end. The flag is on the added line, not the edited one.
hints: Edited lines appear as a < > pair.
diff before.txt after.txt and take the last > line.
example: diff old.conf new.conf
explanation: diff is how you spot tampering, config drift and changes between versions. A line that was edited shows up as a < and > pair. A line that was only added shows up as a > with no partner.
pitfall: Do not include the diff marker when copying a recovered value.
transfer: Why might diff first.txt second.txt && echo identical be useful?
steps: Run diff and read every change.
Pick the line that was added, not the one that was edited.

decoys.hint: That line was edited (it has a < partner in the diff). The flag is on the newly added line at the end.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.

title: Undo a reversed transmission
concept: rev reverses the characters on each line. It's a quick way to undo simple text obfuscation.
brief: reversed.txt contains a transmission sent backwards. Recover the flag. mirror.txt was a test transmission.
hints: rev reversed.txt
Ignore mirror.txt.
example: echo olleh | rev     # prints: hello
explanation: Attackers and puzzle-makers often hide strings with trivial tricks like reversing them. If text reads like gibberish that ends with {REBYC, try rev.
pitfall: rev does not reverse the entire file as one character sequence.
transfer: If a value was reversed and then base64-encoded, which operation should you undo first?
steps: Reverse reversed.txt.

decoys.hint: That's from mirror.txt, the test transmission. Reverse reversed.txt.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.

title: Store the route
concept: A variable stores a value under a name. export DEST=/some/path sets it, and $DEST is replaced by that value in later commands.
brief: Set DEST to /opt/academy/signal, then read the receipt through "$DEST/receipt". Careful: a similarly named folder exists.
hints: There is also /opt/academy/signals (plural). Tab completion may pick it.
export DEST=/opt/academy/signal then cat "$DEST/receipt"
example:
export LOGS=/var/log
ls "$LOGS"
explanation: Variables keep long paths and settings in one place. Use double quotes around "$DEST/file" so paths with spaces still work. In this lab, set the variable in one command and use it in the next.
pitfall: Single quotes around $PLACE print its name literally.
transfer: Why are quotes useful around expanded paths that may contain spaces?
steps: Set the DEST variable to exactly /opt/academy/signal.
Read the receipt using $DEST.

decoys.hint: That's from /opt/academy/signals (plural). DEST must be /opt/academy/signal.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.
Single quotes stop $DEST from expanding. Use double quotes.

title: Traverse a locked directory
concept: For directories, x means permission to enter (traverse) them. Without it you can't reach any file inside, even one you're allowed to read.
brief: The vault directory has lost its owner traverse permission. Restore it and read vault/receipt. The backup copy is stale.
hints: ls -l shows vault as drw-------.
chmod u+x vault then cat vault/receipt
example:
ls -ld vault        # d rw- ... no x for the owner
chmod u+x vault     # allow entering it
explanation: Directory permissions trip up even experienced admins: r lets you list a folder's names, and x lets you go through it. Fixing traversal is often the real answer to a Permission denied error on a file path.
pitfall: Adding read permission to a file does not fix a missing traversal bit on its parent directory.
transfer: Why can a readable file still return permission denied?
steps: Work out why vault/receipt can't be read.
Restore the missing directory permission, then read the receipt.

decoys.hint: That's from vault-backup, which is stale. Fix the vault directory's permissions and read the real receipt.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.

title: Recover after a failed check
concept: && runs the next command only if the previous one succeeded, and || runs it only if the previous one failed. test -f file succeeds when the file exists.
brief: Write one line that creates restored.txt containing recovered, but only if missing.txt does not exist. Use test and ||.
hints: test -f missing.txt fails because the file is absent.
test -f missing.txt || echo recovered > restored.txt
example:
test -f config.ini || echo missing
test -d logs && echo "logs exist"
explanation: Conditionals let a single line react to the system, which is the heart of scripting. command1 || command2 reads as "try this, otherwise do that".
pitfall: Do not judge success only by whether output was printed.
transfer: Which branch executes when test -f missing.txt is false?
steps: Check what test -f missing.txt returns.
Chain it with || so the recovery only runs on failure.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.

title: Count accepted records
concept: wc -l counts lines. Piping grep into wc -l counts how many lines matched.
brief: Count the lines in traffic.txt that begin with ACCEPT and write just that number to count.txt. Some lines contain ACCEPT without starting with it.

files.text:
ACCEPT a
DROP b
ACCEPT c
NOT ACCEPTED x
ACCEPT d
DROP e

hints: grep ACCEPT also matches NOT ACCEPTED.
grep ^ACCEPT traffic.txt | wc -l > count.txt
example: grep ^FAIL auth.log | wc -l
explanation: Counting matches is everyday analysis: how many failed logins, how many dropped packets. Make sure your filter matches only what you mean, because one wrong match changes the answer.
pitfall: A file containing text without a final newline may have fewer newline characters than visible text records.
transfer: Why is filtering before counting different from counting the entire file?
steps: Filter to lines that start with ACCEPT.
Count them and save the number to count.txt.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.

title: Normalize a status stream
concept: tr translates characters: tr A-Z a-z turns every capital letter into lowercase.
brief: Convert status.txt to lowercase and save the result as normalized.txt.
solution: cat status.txt | tr A-Z a-z > normalized.txt
hints: tr only reads standard input.
cat status.txt | tr A-Z a-z > normalized.txt
example: echo HELLO | tr A-Z a-z     # prints: hello
explanation: Normalizing text (same case, same separators) makes data easy to compare and search. tr reads from standard input, so feed it with a pipe or <.
pitfall: Passing a filename to tr does not make it read that file. Redirect or pipe the contents instead.
transfer: When would changing case lose information that should be preserved?
steps: Feed status.txt into tr and translate uppercase to lowercase.
Save the output to normalized.txt.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.
tr doesn't take filenames. Pipe the file in: cat status.txt | tr A-Z a-z

title: Order numeric priorities
concept: sort orders lines alphabetically by default, so 10 comes before 2. sort -n sorts by numeric value instead.
brief: Find the smallest number in priorities.txt and save just that number to first.txt.
hints: Plain sort puts 10 before 2.
sort -n priorities.txt | head -n 1 > first.txt
example: sort -n sizes.txt | head -n 1    # smallest number
explanation: Alphabetical sorting compares character by character, which gives surprising results for numbers. Always use -n for numbers. -r reverses the order.
pitfall: A value that starts with digits is not always semantically a number; a postal code, for example, is an identifier.
transfer: Why can lexical ordering put 10 before 2?
steps: Sort the numbers so the smallest comes first. Check your output.
Save only the first line to first.txt.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.

title: Clean the staging folder
concept: rm deletes files and rmdir deletes empty directories. A glob like staging/*.tmp deletes just the temp files.
brief: Delete the temporary files in staging, then remove the empty staging folder. keep.txt must survive.
hints: rm staging/*.tmp
rmdir staging
example:
ls build/*.tmp     # check first
rm build/*.tmp     # then delete
explanation: Deleting is permanent: there's no recycle bin. Be precise with globs, check with ls before you delete, and prefer rmdir for folders so you only remove them once they're empty.
pitfall: A broad wildcard can match more files than intended. Never use deletion commands without understanding the target path.
transfer: Why is rmdir safer than recursive removal when you expect an empty directory?
steps: Check what's in staging.
Delete the .tmp files, then the empty folder. Leave keep.txt alone.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.
rm -r works here, but rmdir is safer: it refuses to delete a folder that still has files in it.

title: Advanced checkpoint: restore the relay
concept: Combine discovery, filtering, decoding, and evidence preservation. Verify each stage rather than guessing a long command. There can be more than one correct sequence of commands.
brief: Final checkpoint. Several dispatch.dat files exist under /opt/academy. Use the ACTIVE one: select its RELEASE record, decode field 2, and save the decoded flag to /home/user/final.txt.
hints: Each dispatch.dat starts with a STATUS line.
grep RELEASE /opt/academy/sector-9/dispatch.dat | cut -d : -f 2 | base64 -d | tee /home/user/final.txt
example: find /opt/academy -type f
explanation: A capstone brings discovery and transformation together. Keep an evidence trail: know where the source came from, what each pipeline stage changes, and where the final result is saved. Equivalent valid command sequences are accepted because the result matters more than one memorized solution.
pitfall: The final flag must also be saved at the requested path before the mission is complete.
transfer: How would you debug this workflow if you found the file but produced an empty final report?
steps: Find every dispatch.dat under /opt/academy and work out which is ACTIVE.
Decode the RELEASE payload from that file only, and save it to /home/user/final.txt.

decoys.hint: That came from sector-3, which is RETIRED. Check each file's STATUS line and use the ACTIVE one.

coach.tip: That's a flag, not a command. Paste it into the flag box under the terminal.
